newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. slams Colombia's army chief, military justice.
newsitem.headline: U.S. slams Colombia's army chief, military justice.

text.p: The U.S. government launched a stinging attack on Colombia's army chief on Tuesday, a week after he cleared a three-star general of serious human rights violations.
The State Department communique said it hoped Congress would soon pass legislation to revamp the country's military justice system -- frequently criticised by international human rights groups.

Referring to army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett simply as "the military judge", the State Department condemned his comments that the civilian Chief Prosecutor's office rigged evidence against Gen. Farouk Yanine, who was accused of links to the 1987 massacre of 19 merchants in central Colombia.

"We are worried by the tone of the verdict of the military judge, who used strong words to attack the civilian authorities who presented charges against Yanine before the case was handed over to military justice. We watch with concern this type of attack on civilian judicial authorities," the statement said.

The State Department said it was "not in a position to evaluate" the merits of the trial or the verdict, but added: "We understand the Colombian government will present draft legislation to Congress to revise the military penal code ... We hope this legislation meets with international standards."

Late last year both Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International issued reports claiming there were organic links between the Colombian military and right-wing death squads. The groups were also highly critical of Washington for failing to ban arms exports to this Andean nation.

Colombian political analyst Eduardo Pizarro recently described Bonett as a "flexible" military man who realised that Washington's backing for "dirty war" tactics against leftist rebel movements in the 1980s had now turned 180 degrees toward active promotion of human rights.
